answer_text:
We need solve

\[
y''(x)+x^2y'(x)+y(x)^3=0,
\qquad y(0)=0,\quad y'(0)=0.
\]

Rewrite the equation as a first-order system. Let

\[
u_1(x)=y(x),\qquad u_2(x)=y'(x).
\]

Then

\[
u_1'=u_2,
\]
and from the differential equation,

\[
u_2'=-x^2u_2-u_1^3.
\]

So the system is

\[
\begin{cases}
u_1'=u_2,\\[2mm]
u_2'=-x^2u_2-u_1^3,
\end{cases}
\qquad
u_1(0)=0,\quad u_2(0)=0.
\]

The right-hand side

\[
F(x,u_1,u_2)=\bigl(u_2,\,-x^2u_2-u_1^3\bigr)
\]

is a polynomial in \(x,u_1,u_2\), hence is \(C^1\) and locally Lipschitz in \((u_1,u_2)\). Therefore the standard existence and uniqueness theorem for first-order systems applies: the initial value problem has a unique local solution near \(x=0\).

Now observe that

\[
u_1(x)\equiv 0,\qquad u_2(x)\equiv 0
\]

is a solution of the system, since

\[
0'=0,
\]

and

\[
0'=-x^2\cdot 0-0^3=0.
\]

It also satisfies the initial conditions. By uniqueness, this is the only solution satisfying those initial conditions.

Thus

\[
y(x)\equiv 0.
\]

Indeed, \(y\equiv 0\) satisfies the original ODE:

\[
0+0+0=0,
\]

and also \(y(0)=0\), \(y'(0)=0\).

Therefore the solution is

\[
\boxed{y(x)=0\ \text{for all }x.}
\]
